units: the writer is taking a course in making clothes
she signed up as the cold season began
the tutor handed out pieces of cloth at the first session
the first task was hemming a square of cotton without a machine
the earliest attempts were started again on two evenings running

that loose stitching stops the layers from shifting

text: I am writing to you from the sewing workshop I joined as the cold season set in. On the first evening the tutor handed round offcuts of cloth and set us to hemming a square of cotton by hand. My stitches wandered off the line, and I unpicked the lot on two evenings running. The week after, she showed us how to tack the layers together before any proper stitching, which stops them shifting under the needle. The step looks like wasted effort, and it saves a great deal of bother later. Mending came next: I patched a pair of trousers worn through at the knee, setting a heavier piece of canvas underneath. Yesterday I finished a lined skirt, and the tutor called the finish neat. I am coming home with a box of pins, a metal thimble and every intention of carrying on. I shall show you the whole lot when you next call round.

units: little balls forming on a knit come from the length of the fibres
fibres that are too short work their way out of the cloth
rubbing rolls those fibres together
a yarn of long, tightly twisted strands holds up better
the twist keeps the fibre ends inside the yarn
cheap articles wear out faster
how a garment is worn and looked after counts as much as its quality
a strap rubbing repeatedly on a sleeve causes the fault
a fabric shaver or a fine-toothed comb takes the balls off
that clearing leaves the colour slightly paler
text: Why does a jumper start bobbling after no more than three washes? The answer comes down to how long the fibres are. The short ones work their way up to the surface, tangle together under rubbing and roll into those little balls that leave a garment looking tired before its time. A long, tightly twisted yarn holds up far better, since the fibre ends stay locked away inside the twist. So a cheap jumper is doomed from the start? Broadly yes, though how you wear the thing and how you look after it count just as much. A sleeve rubbing all day against a bag strap will bobble in the end, even in a lovely knit. Can any of it be rescued? Certainly. A fabric shaver or a fine-toothed comb lifts the top layer away. That does leave the colour a shade paler, so go gently with the thing.

units: a customer brought in a coat whose inner cloth was coming apart

the closing seam is done without a machine so as to stay discreet

appointments are booked three weeks ahead
text: The man who runs an alterations workshop tells of a customer arriving with a coat whose lining was fraying under the arms. She had written the thing off, he says. The case is a common one: the lining, cut from a light cloth, gives way long before the woollen outer, since it takes all the rubbing at the shoulder. Putting it right takes one session at the machine. He unpicks the armhole, replaces the ruined panel with fresh satin in a matching shade, then closes the seam by hand so that no bulk shows. The coat will go on for another ten years, he adds, and he turns down any estimate that comes to more than the price of a replacement. His diary is full three weeks ahead, a sign that people are coming back to mending. Bring the coat in at the first dropped stitch, he advises.

units: colouring cloth once called for long preparation
the dyes came from crushed plants and animals
two baths one after the other did not give quite the same shade

a metal salt had to be added so the colour would not go at the rinse
chemical dyes overturned that practice

those products stand up to washing and cost far less
old cloth told you about the harvest it came from
the text presents the steadiness gained as a loss of variety
text: Getting a clear, steady colour once called for a patience we have long since mislaid. Dye came out of pounded roots, boiled bark and crushed shells, and no two baths ever yielded quite the same shade. Cloth left the vat uneven and alive, marked by the hand that had lowered it in. The bath had to be fixed with a metal salt as well, or the colour ran away at the first rinse. Dyes born of chemistry overturned all that. They give one shade from roll to roll, they hold through washing, and they cost a fraction of what went before. The gain is real; so is the loss. Where a craftsman once read in a length of cloth the trace of a harvest and a season, we read nothing beyond a shade that can be repeated at will. Our wardrobes gained in evenness what our eyes gave up in surprise.

units: the text sets out three categories of textile material
the first category comes from animals
the fibre taken from a fleece traps air and keeps the cold out
the fibre drawn from a cocoon is smooth and glossy
the filling taken from beneath the feathers is very light and bulky
the second category comes from plants
the fibre from a stem dries quickly but creases
the third category is made industrially
those fibres come either from treated plant matter or from oil
an article combining two categories makes care trickier
text: Three families of fibre share out the contents of our wardrobes between them. The first gathers what comes from animals: wool, taken from a fleece, traps air in its crimp and keeps the cold out; silk, unwound from a cocoon, gives a smooth, glossy surface; down, gathered from beneath the feathers, weighs almost nothing and swells enormously. The second family covers what grows: cotton, drawn from a boll, soaks up moisture; linen, pulled from a stem, dries quickly but creases; hemp takes hard wear. The third is made in the works: some fibres come from treated plant matter, others from oil, and both can be spun as fine as you please. Each family sets its own care, its own wash temperature, its own way of drying. Anything mixing two families together makes that choice harder.

units: a craftsman works in a long-established quarter
a customer came in with a garment torn at the shoulder

the trace showed only under a particular light
text: A tailor with premises in a long-established quarter was visited by a customer whose dress had torn at the shoulder the evening before a ceremony. He studied the tear through a magnifying glass, saw that the weave had given way across a short span, and told her the dress would be saved. He began by setting pins around the weakened area so that nothing could shift. Then he stretched the cloth over a wooden hoop, so the weave would not draw in on itself. He drew a thread out of an inner seam, one matching the colour of the dress exactly, and set about darning the tear stitch by patient stitch. The work took up a good part of the evening. By the end, the damage showed only under a lamp held at a low angle. The customer left without having to give up the outfit she had meant to wear.

units: the warmth of the water decides how washing a woollen knit turns out
water that is too hot opens the scales on the fibre
those open scales catch on one another and pack the knit tight
the garment then shrinks for good
a mild washing product is advised
rubbing and wringing by hand cause the same fault as heat
the water is to be taken out by pressing the garment in absorbent cloth
drying is done flat to avoid the garment losing its shape
this velvety material is not to be soaked but brushed dry
a light surface mark comes off with a rubber made for it
text: Before a woollen jumper goes anywhere near water, check the warmth of the bath, because that is what settles the outcome. Hot water opens the scales on the fibre; the scales then catch on one another, the knit felts, and the garment shrinks for good. Lukewarm water, by contrast, leaves the fibre as it was. A mild soap will do, since alkaline products attack those same scales. Do not rub and do not wring, because agitation felts the wool exactly as heat does. Press the garment between two towels instead, then lay it flat to dry; hung up, it would stretch under its own weight. Brushed leather follows other rules altogether. Soaking hardens its surface, so brush it dry with a soft brush, always in one direction. A light surface mark comes away with a rubber made for the purpose.

text: In the sorting shed the sacks are stacked to the rafters and the smell of damp cloth catches in your throat. Ten tonnes come in every week, and half of it is worth nothing at all, says the woman who runs the place and has been sorting for ten years. The trouble is not the volume, she reckons, but the mixing: a tee shirt putting cotton together with plastic fibre cannot be recycled, because the two will not come apart. So it gets burnt, or shipped abroad. Her answer comes in three parts. Garments made from one material only; a label anyone can read, setting out exactly what is in the thing; and mending workshops close to the collection points. Two neighbouring towns have opened such a workshop, and the volume for destruction has dropped sharply. She hopes others will follow.

units: two outdoor garments hang next to each other

that garment is heavy and will last several cold seasons
the second is made of a coated fabric in a strong colour
the second squashes down enough to fit in a pocket

the second protects poorly once the air goes still
the woollen cloth covers itself in little balls while the fabric cracks at the folds
text: Two coats hanging side by side on the same rail turn out to have almost nothing in common. The first is cut from a thick woollen cloth in a deep grey, with a surface that drags at the hand like felt. Its seams are doubled, its buttons sewn through four holes, its collar rises right up to the jaw. It sits heavily on the shoulder, and it will last several winters without weakening. The second, in coated fabric of a bright blue, crumples up in a fist and folds away into a pocket. Its shiny lining slides along the sleeves and its zip runs unbroken from hem to chin. It cuts the wind better than its neighbour, yet it lets the cold through the moment the air goes still. The woollen cloth bobbles in patches, while the coated fabric cracks along the folds. One protects by its bulk, the other by its skin.

units: the shoulder of a jacket reveals how well it was made

the quality of the material is judged on the inner face of the cloth
you have to check whether the weave is tight or slack
the openings for buttons should have clean, even edges
the writer advises checking before buying whether the garment can be mended
an article with no part that can be replaced is not recommended
the writer judges that inability to mend an expensive thing
text: Nothing gives a wardrobe away like the shoulder of a jacket. Look at it from an angle: if the seam falls straight, somebody thought about the garment; if it caves in, it came off a line by the mile. The cut is judged in a second, before your hand ever reaches the cloth. The cloth itself is read on the wrong side, where you find out whether the weave is tight or slack. The finishing is read in the buttonholes, whose edges ought to be closed and even. Care, last of all, is settled at the moment of buying: a garment whose button cannot be changed and whose lining cannot be restitched deserves no attachment. A replaced lining wears as well as the first, provided a seam gives the needle something to grip. We wear things we would be helpless to mend, and that helplessness costs us more than we care to admit.
